newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: FOCUS- Ivory Coast fails to secure IMF loan deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Ivory Coast fails to secure IMF loan deal.

text.p: An IMF team has left Ivory Coast without agreeing a new structural adjustment programme with the government, which will delay a series of badly-needed debt reduction deals, donor sources said on Monday.

One source said that agreement had been reached on liberalising the cocoa and coffee sectors -- a central demand of the International Monetary Fund and other donors -- but there were a few other sticking points, which he declined to detail.
"The talks have not quite finished. There are a couple of things to resolve," he said.
Ivory Coast, the world's biggest producer of cocoa and a major coffee producer -- has reluctantly agreed to a complete reform of its Caistab commodities marketing board.
"There will be no bareme (official list of marketing prices) and no indicative minimum reference prices," the source said.
The private sector would be in charge of export auctions for coffee and for cocoa from 1999 at the latest.
The prices paid to peasant farmers are likely to go up as a result of the reforms, going some way to alleviating rural poverty in Ivory Coast, a major concern of the World Bank.
Budget transparency, unwise investment in certain infrastructure projects and corruption were also mentioned by donor sources as matters of concern.

The IMF team has left Abidjan, and even though the two sides would be exchanging information over the next week, it was "extremely unlikely" that a draft deal would be ready for the next IMF board meeting in September, one source said.
After that, IMF and World Bank officials will be preoccupied by their annual meetings, to be held this year in Hong Kong.
That does not exclude a deal in October, but the timetable for freeing loan funds during the current year would be tight.

Securing an IMF Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) is vital if Ivory Coast is to get a further rescheduling of its official debt owed to governments in the Paris Club, and for its hopes of securing a wider debt write-off under the donor community's Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative.
Analysts also noted that an IMF deal was needed to secure from donors the "up-front" money to implement a hard-won debt reduction deal with commercial banks signed in May.
However, one bank analyst said he doubted that the donors and the Ivory Coast government were too far apart.

"If the problem had been over the Caistab, I would have been worried, but it looks like the big issues have been sorted out," he said, adding he was impressed with the achievements of the Ivorian government over the past three years.
Ivory Coast's previous structural adjustment programme, covering the three years from March 1994, was signed just after the 50 percent devaluation of the CFA franc in January 1994.
The IMF and World Bank had been pressing for years for the devaluation of the Franc Zone's common currency, and donors supported the move with big loans and debt relief packages.

According to official sources, the country's efforts to turn around its finances have been rewarded with a growing primary budget surplus, but that achievement is wiped out by debt servicing, which still swallows over 60 percent of tax revenue.
